title: Policy Gradient Methods
oneLiner: Skip the value table and learn the action probabilities directly: make actions that turned out well more likely, and keep each change small enough to stay stable.

what.html:
Policy-gradient methods give the agent an adjustable strategy (a policy with parameters θ) that outputs probabilities of actions. After acting, they nudge θ so that actions followed by good outcomes become more likely and bad ones less likely. REINFORCE does this with whole-episode returns; actor–critic adds a learned critic to judge actions step by step; PPO limits each update so learning stays stable.

Everyday versionA basketball player adjusts their shooting technique a little after each shot: more of what went in, less of what missed, without ever writing down a "value" for every position on the court.

why.html:
• Works for continuous actions like steering angles or joint torques.
  • Can learn deliberately random strategies when those are best.
  • PPO is the default in much of modern deep RL, including fine-tuning chatbots.

how.title: Sometimes the best strategy is random
how.html: If three corridor cells look identical but one reverses your controls, any fixed "always right" or "always left" rule gets stuck forever. Going right 59% of the time is best. Value-based greedy methods can't express that; policies can.

how.title: Turning preferences into probabilities
how.html: For a few actions: give each a preference score and apply a softmax. For continuous actions: output a mean and a spread and sample from a bell curve.

how.title: The key trick
how.html: The policy gradient theorem says: the direction to improve is the average of (how good the action was) × (the direction that makes that action more likely). You can estimate it just by playing, with no model of the world.

how.title: REINFORCE
how.html: After an episode, for each action taken: θ += α × return × (direction that makes it more likely). With preferences (0.5, −0.2), return 2 and α = 0.1, they become (0.566, −0.266).

how.title: Compare with what's typical
how.html: Subtract a baseline (e.g. the average return) so only better-than-usual actions get pushed up. Same direction on average, much less noise.

how.title: Actor and critic
how.html: The actor picks actions; the critic estimates values. After each step the critic's TD error says "better or worse than expected?", and the actor adjusts immediately.

how.title: Small, safe steps: PPO
how.html: PPO caps how much more (or less) likely an action may become in one update: the probability ratio is clipped to [0.8, 1.2]. A good action pushed to ratio 1.3 only gets credit for 1.2: min(3.9, 3.6) = 3.6.

how.title: Continuous control
how.html: DDPG, TD3 and SAC combine a policy with Q-critics and replay memory for robots and other continuous tasks. SAC also rewards keeping the policy random enough to explore.

demo.html: Run REINFORCE on the corridor with and without a baseline. The baseline version can use a 10× bigger step and learns much faster.

example.html:
One REINFORCE step. Two actions with preferences 0.5 and −0.2 give probabilities 0.668 and 0.332. The first action was taken and the return was 2. The "make it more likely" direction is (1 − 0.668, 0 − 0.332) = (0.332, −0.332). With α = 0.1: preferences (0.566, −0.266), so the first action is now a bit more likely.

Supplementary If every return is negative (−1 per step), REINFORCE without a baseline pushes every taken action down; only the differences matter, which is exactly what a baseline provides.

misunderstandings: Policy gradients need a model to differentiate.
The score-function trick only needs samples.
With aliasing or opponents, randomness can be optimal.
PPO's clip limits the parameter change.
It limits the change in action probabilities (the ratio).
takeaways: Learn π(a|s, θ) directly; softmax for discrete, Gaussian for continuous actions.
REINFORCE uses Gₜ; baselines cut variance; actor–critic uses TD errors.
TRPO/PPO limit each policy change (worked PPO: 3.6).
DDPG, TD3, SAC for continuous control.
thirty: Policy-gradient methods parameterise π(a|s, θ), e.g. a softmax over preferences or a Gaussian for continuous actions, and ascend J(θ). The policy gradient theorem gives ∇J ∝ E[q_π(S, A)∇ln π(A|S, θ)], estimable from samples via the log-derivative trick. REINFORCE uses the return Gₜ (worked: θ = [0.5, −0.2] → [0.566, −0.266] for G = 2); subtracting a baseline such as v̂(s) keeps the gradient unbiased and reduces variance, giving advantage estimates; actor–critic uses the critic's TD error online. Stochastic optimal policies arise with aliasing (short corridor, p ≈ 0.59). Natural gradients and TRPO constrain the KL change; PPO clips the ratio rₜ to [1 − ε, 1 + ε] (r = 1.3, A = 3, ε = 0.2 → 3.6). DDPG, TD3 and SAC are off-policy actor–critics for continuous control.
